analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress, lobbyists, and federal agencies to post their financial disclosures, earmarks, lobbying contacts, and documents online where the public can read them.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2010 with a single cosponsor, the bill was sent to five House committees, never reached a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have opened up how Washington works. Members of Congress would have to post their big personal financial transactions, gifts, foreign travel reports, and every earmark request — who gets the money, how much, and why — on public websites within hours. Lobbyists would have to register faster, name every official they contact, and disclose bundled campaign contributions. Bills and conference reports would have to be posted online for 72 hours before Congress could vote on them, and agencies would have to put their research reports and completed Freedom of Information Act responses online for free. It died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, journalists, and watchdog groups gain access to information now held inside the building: searchable databases of Members' financial disclosures, earmark requests, committee votes and schedules, the full text of legislation 72 hours before votes, Congressional Research Service reports, completed FOIA responses, and detailed federal contract data. Taxpayers also gain visibility into who requests earmarks and which contractors win federal money and how.

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress would have to post quarterly reports of large personal financial transactions, and all financial disclosure, travel, and gift reports would be posted online within 48 hours in searchable form.

Any Member requesting an earmark, limited tax benefit, or limited tariff benefit would have to post the recipient, whether it is for-profit, the amount, and a justification on their own website within 24 hours, with all requests compiled into a centralized public database.
Bills and conference reports could not be considered in the House until their full text had been publicly available online for 72 hours, so citizens could read a law before it was voted on.

Congressional Research Service reports prepared for Members would be made public online, and agencies would have to post completed Freedom of Information Act responses electronically, free of charge, within a month.

Lobbyists would face faster registration (72 hours instead of 45 days), a lower registration threshold, mandatory identification of every executive and legislative official they contact, and quarterly disclosure of bundled campaign contributions.
Federal contracting data would be expanded and audited annually, with contractor performance and misconduct records made searchable and public for a 10-year lookback.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress would bear new disclosure of their finances and earmarks; lobbyists face faster registration, lower thresholds, and must reveal who they contact and the contributions they bundle; federal contractors would have their competition history, profit incentives, and 10-year performance and misconduct records posted publicly; congressional committees and agencies would bear the cost of building and maintaining the new public databases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress, lobbyists, and federal contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the smallest dollar band for reporting personal financial items from $15,000 to $25,000, so lower-value holdings and transactions would be reported with less detail than under existing law.

Quarterly financial transaction reports are required only for transactions of $250,000 or more by the Member, spouse, or dependent child; most stock trades by Members would still only be disclosed on the annual filing.

The CRS public-access requirement exempts information deemed confidential by the CRS Director or a providing agency, and the 72-hour rule for posting legislation excludes classified material, leaving room for withholdings.
The 72-hour rule before House consideration of bills and conference reports would delay action even when Congress needs to move quickly, and waivers would require a two-thirds vote on the rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but indirect: the bill changes what citizens can see, not what the government does, and its value depends on journalists, watchdogs, and voters actually using the data. The costs are modest — mostly compliance work for congressional offices, committees, and agencies, and a small delay (up to 72 hours) before legislation can be considered, which could slow emergency responses. The largest honest objection is that it stops short: quarterly trade disclosure applies only to transactions of $250,000 or more, and confidentiality carve-outs leave room for withholding. As a transparency bill it is well-aimed; its fatal weakness was political, not design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced; none of them ever brought it up, and the Congress ended without a vote on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Quigley introduced the Transparency in Government Act of 2010 on March 25, 2010, and it was referred the same day to five committees: Oversight and Government Reform, Rules, House Administration, Judiciary, and Standards of Official Conduct.
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a House Democrat, over the life of the bill.

On June 15, 2010, the Judiciary Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; the action history records no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point.

The bill would have required bills and conference reports to be publicly available online for 72 hours before House consideration, quarterly online disclosure of large Members' financial transactions, 24-hour posting of every earmark request, and expanded lobbying and federal contracting disclosure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people the bill would have exposed are better off: Members who would have had to post their financial trades and earmark requests, and lobbyists who would have faced faster registration and disclosure of their contacts and bundled contributions, avoided all of the new requirements, while the public never received the disclosures.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, but because it never reached a committee vote or floor vote, no partisan breakdown was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would halve the registration threshold to $5,000, force registration within 72 hours of starting to lobby, require naming every official contacted, and require quarterly disclosure of bundled campaign contributions [S3]. A GAO study would probe whether influencers are dodging registration altogether [S3]. These requirements make lobbying work more visible and more expensive to do quietly.

Contract and grant data on the federal spending website would be expanded to include competition details, profit incentives, and noncompete rationales, with annual external data audits [S3]. The contractor performance and integrity database would become public and cover 10 years of records, including settlements without fault findings [S3].

Members would face quarterly reporting of large personal financial transactions, online posting of gift and travel reports within 48 hours, and 24-hour public posting of every earmark request with recipient and dollar amount, plus a House rule barring consideration of bills containing undisclosed earmarks [S3].
